mn100:1.2: On one occasion the Blessed One was wandering in the Kosalan country with a large Sangha of bhikkhus.
mn100:2.1: Now on that occasion a brahmin woman named Dhanañjānī was living at Caṇḍalakappa; she had full confidence in the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Sangha.
mn100:2.2: Then the brahmin woman Dhanañjānī, having stumbled, uttered this exclamation three times:
mn100:2.3: “Homage to that Blessed One, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One.
mn100:2.4: Homage to that Blessed One, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One.
mn100:2.5: Homage to that Blessed One, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One.”
mn100:3.1: Now on that occasion a student named Saṅgārava was living at Caṇḍalakappa, an expert in the Three Vedas, together with their vocabularies, ritual, phonology, and etymology, and the histories as a fifth; skilled in philology and grammar, and fully versed in natural philosophy and in the marks of a great man.
mn100:3.2: The student Saṅgārava heard the brahmin woman Dhanañjānī speaking these words.
mn100:3.3: Having heard this, he said to the brahmin woman Dhanañjānī:
mn100:3.4: “This brahmin woman Dhanañjānī is degraded indeed, this brahmin woman Dhanañjānī is disgraced indeed, that when there are brahmins possessing the three knowledges, she praises that shaveling ascetic.”
mn100:3.5: “You do not know, dear sir, that Blessed One’s virtue and wisdom.
mn100:3.6: If you knew, dear sir, that Blessed One’s virtue and wisdom, you would not think that that Blessed One should be abused and reviled.”
mn100:3.7: “Well then, madam, when the ascetic Gotama arrives at Caṇḍalakappa, tell me.”
mn100:3.8: “Yes, dear sir,” the brahmin woman Dhanañjānī replied to the student Saṅgārava.
mn100:4.1: Then the Blessed One, wandering by stages through the Kosalan country, arrived at Caṇḍalakappa.
mn100:4.2: There the Blessed One stayed at Caṇḍalakappa, in the mango grove of the Todeyya brahmins.
mn100:5.1: The brahmin woman Dhanañjānī heard: “The Blessed One, it seems, has arrived at Caṇḍalakappa, and is staying at Caṇḍalakappa, in the mango grove of the Todeyya brahmins.”
mn100:5.2: Then the brahmin woman Dhanañjānī went to the student Saṅgārava and said to him:
mn100:5.3: “Dear sir, that Blessed One has arrived at Caṇḍalakappa, and is staying at Caṇḍalakappa, in the mango grove of the Todeyya brahmins.
mn100:5.4: Now, dear sir, it is time for you to do as you think fit.”
mn100:5.5: “Yes, madam,” the student Saṅgārava replied to the brahmin woman Dhanañjānī, and he went to the Blessed One and exchanged greetings with him.
mn100:5.6: When the courteous and amiable talk was finished, he sat down at one side. When he had done so, the student Saṅgārava said to the Blessed One:
mn100:6.1: “Master Gotama, there are some ascetics and brahmins who, having reached here and now the consummation and perfection of direct knowledge, claim the fundamentals of the life divine.[^1]
mn100:6.2: Now, Master Gotama, of those ascetics and brahmins who, having reached here and now the consummation and perfection of direct knowledge, claim the fundamentals of the life divine, to which does Master Gotama belong?”
mn100:7.1: “Bhāradvāja, I say that there is diversity even among those who, having reached here and now the consummation and perfection of direct knowledge, claim the fundamentals of the life divine.
mn100:7.2: There are, Bhāradvāja, some ascetics and brahmins who rely on oral tradition.
mn100:7.3: They, on the basis of oral tradition, having reached here and now the consummation and perfection of direct knowledge, claim the fundamentals of the life divine;
mn100:7.4: such are the brahmins who are masters of the Three Vedas.
mn100:7.5: There are, Bhāradvāja, some ascetics and brahmins who, on the basis of mere faith alone, having reached here and now the consummation and perfection of direct knowledge, claim the fundamentals of the life divine;
mn100:7.6: such are the rationalists and investigators.
mn100:7.7: There are, Bhāradvāja, some ascetics and brahmins who, having directly known for themselves a Dhamma among things not heard before, have reached here and now the consummation and perfection of direct knowledge, and claim the fundamentals of the life divine.
mn100:7.8: Of these, Bhāradvāja, the ascetics and brahmins who, having directly known for themselves a Dhamma among things not heard before, have reached here and now the consummation and perfection of direct knowledge, and claim the fundamentals of the life divine—I am one of them.
mn100:8.1: This too, Bhāradvāja, may be understood in such a way that I am one of those ascetics and brahmins who, having directly known for themselves a Dhamma among things not heard before, have reached here and now the consummation and perfection of direct knowledge, and claim the fundamentals of the life divine.
mn100:9.1: Here, Bhāradvāja, before my enlightenment, while I was still a Bodhisatta, not yet fully enlightened, it occurred to me:
mn100:9.2: ‘Household life is crowded and dusty; life gone forth is wide open.
mn100:9.3: It is not easy, while living in a house, to lead the life divine utterly perfect and utterly pure as a polished shell.
mn100:9.4: Suppose I were to shave off my hair and beard, put on the yellow robe, and go forth from the home life into homelessness?’
mn100:9.5: Later, while still a boy, a black-haired youth endowed with the blessing of youth, in the first phase of life, I shaved off my hair and beard—though my mother and father wished otherwise and grieved with tearful faces—I put on the yellow cloth and went forth from the house life into homelessness.
mn100:9.6: Having gone forth in search of what is profitable, seeking the supreme state of sublime peace, I went to Āḷāra Kālāma and I said to him:
mn100:9.7: ‘Friend Kālāma, I want to lead the life divine in this Dhamma and Discipline.’
mn100:9.8: When this was said, Āḷāra Kālāma replied:
mn100:9.10: This Dhamma is such that in no long time a wise man can enter upon and abide in it, himself realizing through direct knowledge his own teacher’s doctrine.’
mn100:9.12: I claimed that as far as mere lip-reciting and rehearsal of his teachings went I could speak with knowledge and assurance, and that I knew and saw—and there were others that did likewise.
mn100:9.14: ‘It is not through mere faith alone the Āḷāra Kālāma declares his Dhamma; (he does so) because he enters upon and abides in it, himself realizing it through direct knowledge.
mn100:9.15: Certainly Āḷāra Kālāma abides in this Dhamma knowing and seeing.’
mn100:10.1: Then I went to Āḷāra Kālāma, and I said to him:
mn100:10.2: ‘Friend Kālāma, in what way do you declare to have entered upon this Dhamma, yourself realizing it through direct knowledge?’
mn100:10.3: When this was said, he declared the base consisting of nothingness.
mn100:10.5: ‘Not only Āḷāra Kālāma has faith; I too have faith.
mn100:10.6: Not only Āḷāra Kālāma has energy …
mn100:10.10: Suppose I exercise control in order to realize the Dhamma that he declares to have entered upon, himself realizing it through direct knowledge?’
mn100:10.11: I soon entered upon and abode in that Dhamma, myself realizing it through direct knowledge.
mn100:10.12: Then I went to Āḷāra Kālāma, and I said to him:
mn100:10.13: ‘Friend Kālāma, is it in this way that you declare to have entered upon this Dhamma, yourself realizing it through direct knowledge?’
mn100:10.14: ‘It is in this way, friend, that I declare to have entered upon this Dhamma, myself realizing it through direct knowledge.’
mn100:10.15: ‘Friend, I too in this way enter upon and abide in this Dhamma, myself realizing it through direct knowledge.’
mn100:10.16: ‘It is gain for us, friend, it is great gain for us,
mn100:10.17: that we have such a venerable one as our companion in the life divine.
mn100:10.18: So the Dhamma that I declare to have entered upon, myself realizing it through direct knowledge, that Dhamma you enter upon and abide in, yourself realizing it through direct knowledge.
mn100:10.19: And the Dhamma that you enter upon and abide in, yourself realizing it through direct knowledge, that Dhamma I declare to have entered upon, myself realizing it through direct knowledge.
mn100:10.20: So you know the Dhamma that I know; I know the Dhamma that you know.
mn100:10.21: As I am, so you are; as you are, so am I.
mn100:10.22: Come, friend, let us now lead this community together.’
mn100:10.23: Thus Āḷāra Kālāma, my Teacher, placed me, his pupil, on an equal footing with himself, and awarded me the highest honour.
mn100:10.25: ‘This Dhamma does not lead to dispassion, to fading of lust, to cessation, to peace, to direct knowledge, to full enlightenment, to Nibbāna, but only to the base consisting of nothingness.’
mn100:10.26: I was not satisfied with that Dhamma. I left it and went away.
mn100:11.1: Still in search of what is profitable, seeking the supreme state of sublime peace, I went to Uddaka Rāmaputta, and I said to him:
mn100:11.2: ‘Friend, I want to lead the life divine in this Dhamma and Discipline.’
mn100:11.3: When this was said, Uddaka Rāmaputta replied:
mn100:11.5: This Dhamma is such that in no long time a wise man can enter upon and abide in it, himself realizing through direct knowledge his own teacher’s doctrine.’
mn100:11.7: I claimed that as far as mere lip-reciting and rehearsal of his teaching went I could speak with knowledge and assurance, and that I knew and saw—and there were others who did likewise.

mn100:11.10: Certainly Rāma abides in this Dhamma knowing and seeing.’
mn100:11.11: Then I went to Uddaka Rāmaputta, and I said to him:
mn100:11.12: ‘Friend Rāma, in what way do you declare to have entered upon this Dhamma, yourself realizing it through direct knowledge?’
mn100:11.13: When this was said, he declared the base consisting of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
mn100:11.15: ‘Not only Rāma has faith; I too have faith.

mn100:11.21: I soon entered upon and abode in that Dhamma, myself realizing it through direct knowledge.

mn100:12.3: ‘It is in this way, friend, that Rāma declared to have entered upon this Dhamma, himself realizing it through direct knowledge.’

mn100:12.7: So the Dhamma that Rāma declared to have entered upon, myself realizing it through direct knowledge, that Dhamma you enter upon and abide in, yourself realizing it through direct knowledge.
mn100:12.8: And the Dhamma that you enter upon and abide in, yourself realizing it through direct knowledge, that Dhamma Rāma declared to have entered upon, himself realizing it through direct knowledge.
mn100:12.9: So you know the Dhamma that Rāma knew directly; Rāma knew directly the Dhamma that you know.
mn100:12.10: As Rāma was, so you are; as you are, so Rāma was.
mn100:12.11: Come, friend, now lead this community.’
mn100:12.12: Thus Uddaka Rāmaputta, my companion in the life divine, placed me in the Teacher’s place, and awarded me the highest honour.
mn100:12.14: ‘This Dhamma does not lead to dispassion, to fading of lust, to cessation, to peace, to direct knowledge, to full enlightenment, to Nibbāna, but only to the base consisting of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.’
mn100:12.15: I was not satisfied with that Dhamma. I left it and went away.
mn100:13.1: Still in search of what is profitable, seeking the supreme state of sublime peace, I wandered by stages through the Magadhan country, till at length I arrived at Senānigama near Uruvelā.
mn100:13.2: There I saw an agreeable piece of ground, a delightful grove, a clear-flowing river with pleasant smooth banks, and nearby a village as alms resort.
mn100:13.4: ‘There is this agreeable piece of ground, this delightful grove, this clear-flowing river with pleasant smooth banks, and nearby a village for alms resort.
mn100:13.5: This will serve for the endeavour of a clansman who seeks endeavour.’
mn100:14.1: Now these three similes occurred to me spontaneously, never heard before.
mn100:14.2: Suppose there were a wet, sappy piece of wood lying in water,
mn100:14.3: and a man came with an upper fire-stick, thinking:
mn100:14.4: ‘I shall light a fire, I shall produce heat’;
mn100:14.5: how do you conceive this, Bhāradvāja,
mn100:14.6: would the man light a fire and produce heat by taking the upper fire-stick and rubbing with it the wet, sappy piece of wood lying in water?”
mn100:14.9: Because it is a wet, sappy piece of wood, and besides, it is lying in water.
mn100:14.10: So the man would reap weariness and disappointment.”
mn100:14.11: “So too, Bhāradvāja, while any ascetics or brahmins live still bodily and mentally not withdrawn from sensual desires, and while their lust, affection, passion, thirst, and fever for sensual desires are not thoroughly abandoned and quieted within them, then even if those good ascetics and brahmins feel painful, racking, piercing feelings due to striving, they are incapable of knowledge, vision, and supreme enlightenment; and even if those good ascetics and brahmins do not feel painful, racking, piercing feelings due to striving, they are incapable of knowledge, vision, and supreme enlightenment.
mn100:14.12: This was the first simile that occurred to me spontaneously, never heard before.
mn100:15.1: Again, a second simile occurred to me spontaneously, never heard before.
mn100:15.2: Suppose there were a wet, sappy piece of wood lying on dry land far from water,
mn100:15.3: and a man came with an upper fire-stick, thinking:
mn100:15.4: ‘I shall light a fire, I shall produce heat’;
mn100:15.5: how do you conceive this, Bhāradvāja,
mn100:15.6: would the man light a fire and produce heat by taking the upper fire-stick and rubbing with it the wet, sappy piece of wood lying on dry land far from water?”
mn100:15.9: Because it is a wet, sappy piece of wood, though it is lying on dry land far from water.
mn100:15.10: So the man would reap weariness and disappointment.” “So too, Bhāradvāja, while any ascetics or brahmins live only bodily withdrawn from sensual desires, and while their lust, affection, passion, thirst, and fever for sensual desires are not thoroughly abandoned and quieted within them, then even if those good ascetics and brahmins feel painful, racking, piercing feelings due to striving, they are incapable of knowledge, vision, and supreme enlightenment. And even if those good ascetics and brahmins do not feel painful, racking, piercing feelings due to striving, they are incapable of knowledge, vision, and supreme enlightenment.
mn100:15.11: This was the second simile that occurred to me spontaneously, never heard before.
mn100:16.1: Again, a third simile occurred to me spontaneously, never heard before.
mn100:16.2: Suppose there were a dry, sapless piece of wood lying on dry land far from water,
mn100:16.3: and a man came with an upper fire-stick, thinking:
mn100:16.4: ‘I shall light a fire, I shall produce heat’;
mn100:16.5: how do you conceive this, Bhāradvāja,
mn100:16.6: would the man light a fire and produce heat by taking the upper fire-stick and rubbing with it the dry, sapless piece of wood lying on dry land far from water?”
mn100:16.9: Because it is a dry, sapless piece of wood, and besides, it is lying on dry land far from water!”
mn100:16.10: “So too, Bhāradvāja, while any ascetics or brahmins live both bodily and mentally withdrawn from sensual desires, and while their lust, affection, passion, thirst, and fever for sensual desires are thoroughly abandoned and quieted within them, then even if those good ascetics and brahmins feel painful, racking, piercing feelings due to striving, they are capable of knowledge, vision, and supreme enlightenment, and even if those good ascetics and brahmins do not feel painful, racking, piercing feelings due to striving, they are capable of knowledge, vision, and supreme enlightenment.
mn100:16.11: This was the third simile that occurred to me spontaneously, never heard before.
mn100:16.12: These, Bhāradvāja, were the three similes that occurred to me spontaneously, never heard before.
mn100:17.2: ‘Suppose, with my teeth clenched and my tongue pressed against the roof of my mouth, I beat down, constrain, and crush mind with mind?’
mn100:17.3: So, with my teeth clenched and my tongue pressed against the roof of my mouth, I beat down, constrained, and crushed mind with mind.
mn100:17.4: While I did so, sweat ran from my armpits.
mn100:17.5: Just as a strong man might seize a weaker man by the head or shoulders and beat him down, constrain, and crush him,
mn100:17.6: so too, while with my teeth clenched and my tongue pressed against the roof of my mouth, I beat down, constrained, and crushed mind with mind, sweat ran from my armpits.
mn100:17.7: But energy was aroused in me, unremitting, and mindfulness was established, unconfused; yet my body was overwrought and not calm, because I was exhausted by that painful striving.
mn100:18.2: ‘Suppose I were to practise the breathless meditation?’
mn100:18.3: So I stopped the in-breaths and out-breaths through my mouth and nose.
mn100:18.4: While I did so, there was a loud sound of winds escaping through my ear-holes.
mn100:18.5: Just as there is a loud sound when a smith’s bellows are blown,
mn100:18.6: so too, while I stopped the in-breaths and out-breaths through my mouth and nose, there was a loud sound of winds escaping through my ear-holes.
mn100:18.7: But energy was aroused in me, unremitting, and mindfulness was established, unconfused; yet my body was overwrought and not calm, because I was exhausted by that painful striving.
mn100:19.2: ‘Suppose I were to practise the breathless meditation further?’
mn100:19.3: So I stopped the in-breaths and out-breaths through my mouth, nose, and ears.
mn100:19.4: While I did so, violent winds struck against my head.
mn100:19.5: Just as if a strong man were splitting my head open with a sharp point,
mn100:19.6: so too, while I stopped the in-breaths and out-breaths through my mouth, nose, and ears, violent winds struck against my head.
mn100:19.7: But energy was aroused in me, unremitting, and mindfulness was established, unconfused; yet my body was overwrought and not calm, because I was exhausted by that painful striving.
mn100:20.2: ‘Suppose I were to practise the breathless meditation further?’
mn100:20.3: So I stopped the in-breaths and out-breaths through my mouth, nose, and ears.
mn100:20.4: While I did so, there were violent pains in my head.
mn100:20.5: Just as if a strong man were tightening a tough leather strap round my head as a headband,
mn100:20.6: so too, while I stopped the in-breaths and out-breaths through my mouth, nose, and ears, there were violent pains in my head.
mn100:20.7: But energy was aroused in me, unremitting, and mindfulness was established, unconfused; yet my body was overwrought and not calm, because I was exhausted by that painful striving.
mn100:21.2: ‘Suppose I were to practise the breathless meditation further?’
mn100:21.3: So I stopped the in-breaths and out-breaths through my mouth, nose, and ears.
mn100:21.4: While I did so, violent winds carved through my belly.
mn100:21.5: Just as a skilled butcher or his apprentice might carve through the belly of an ox with a sharp butcher’s knife,
mn100:21.6: so too, while I stopped the in-breaths and out-breaths through my mouth, nose, and ears, violent winds carved through my belly.
mn100:21.7: But energy was aroused in me, unremitting, and mindfulness was established, unconfused; yet my body was overwrought and not calm, because I was exhausted by that painful striving.
mn100:22.2: ‘Suppose I were to practise the breathless meditation further?’
mn100:22.3: So I stopped the in-breaths and out-breaths through my mouth, nose, and ears.
mn100:22.4: While I did so, there was a violent burning in my body.
mn100:22.5: Just as if two strong men were to seize a weaker man by both arms and roast him, thoroughly roast him, over a pit of burning coals,
mn100:22.6: so too, while I stopped the in-breaths and out-breaths through my mouth, nose, and ears, there was a violent burning in my body.
mn100:22.7: But energy was aroused in me, unremitting, and mindfulness was established, unconfused; yet my body was overwrought and not calm, because I was exhausted by that painful striving.
mn100:23.1: Then, Bhāradvāja, some deities, seeing me, said:
mn100:23.4: ‘The ascetic Gotama is not dead, but he is dying.’
mn100:23.6: ‘The ascetic Gotama is neither dead nor dying;
mn100:23.7: the ascetic Gotama is an Arahant, for such is the way an Arahant abides.’
mn100:24.2: ‘Suppose I were to practise entirely cutting off food?’
mn100:24.3: Then deities came to me and said:
mn100:24.4: ‘Good sir, do not practise entirely cutting off food.
mn100:24.5: If you do so, good sir, we shall infuse heavenly essence into you through your pores,
mn100:24.6: and you will live on that.’
mn100:24.8: ‘If I were to claim to be completely fasting, and these deities were to infuse heavenly essence into me through my pores, and I were to live on that,
mn100:24.9: that would be false speech on my part.’
mn100:24.10: So I refused those deities, saying: ‘Enough.’
mn100:25.2: ‘Suppose I were to take very little food, a handful at a time, whether bean soup, or lentil soup, or vetch soup, or pea soup?’
mn100:25.3: So I took very little food, a handful at a time, whether bean soup, or lentil soup, or vetch soup, or pea soup.
mn100:25.4: While I took very little food in this way, my body reached a state of extreme emaciation.
mn100:25.5: Just like the jointed segments of vine stems or bamboo stems, so my limbs became, because of eating so little.
mn100:25.6: Just like a camel’s hoof, so my backside became, because of eating so little;
mn100:25.7: just like a string of beads, so my spine, with its projections standing up and sinking down, became, because of eating so little.
mn100:25.8: Just as the rafters of an old barn collapse and jut out, so my ribs, collapsing and jutting out, became, because of eating so little.
mn100:25.9: Just as the sparkle of water sunk far down and deep in a deep well appears, so the sparkle of my eyes, sunk far down and deep in their sockets, appeared, because of eating so little.
mn100:25.10: Just as a bitter gourd, cut green, shrivels and withers in the wind and sun, so my scalp, shrivelling and withering, became, because of eating so little.
mn100:25.11: When I thought, ‘I will touch the skin of my belly,’ I actually took hold of my spine as well; and when I thought, ‘I will touch my spine,’ I actually took hold of the skin of my belly as well; so much had the skin of my belly become stuck to my spine, because of eating so little.
mn100:25.12: When I thought, ‘I will move my bowels or pass water,’ I fell down on my face right there, because of eating so little.
mn100:25.13: When, trying to ease my body, I stroked my limbs with my hand, the hairs, rotted at their roots, fell away from my body, because of eating so little.
mn100:26.1: Then, Bhāradvāja, some people, seeing me, said: ‘The ascetic Gotama is black.’
mn100:26.2: Some people said: ‘The ascetic Gotama is not black, the ascetic Gotama is brown.’
mn100:26.3: Some people said: ‘The ascetic Gotama is neither black nor brown, the ascetic Gotama is golden-skinned’;
mn100:26.4: so much had the clear, bright colour of my skin deteriorated, because of eating so little.
mn100:27.2: ‘Whatever ascetics or brahmins in the past have felt painful, racking, piercing feelings due to striving, this is the utmost, there is none beyond this;
mn100:27.3: whatever ascetics or brahmins in the future will feel painful, racking, piercing feelings due to striving, this is the utmost, there is none beyond this;
mn100:27.4: and whatever ascetics or brahmins at present feel painful, racking, piercing feelings due to striving, this is the utmost, there is none beyond this.
mn100:27.5: But by this severe austerity I have not attained any superhuman state, any distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones.
mn100:27.6: Might there be another path to enlightenment?’
mn100:28.2: ‘I recall that, while my father the Sakyan was working, sitting in the cool shade of a rose-apple tree, quite secluded from sensual desires, secluded from unwholesome states, I entered upon and abided in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by initial application and sustained application, with joy and pleasure born of seclusion.
mn100:28.3: Might this be the path to enlightenment?’
mn100:28.4: Then, following on that memory, came the recognition:
mn100:29.2: ‘Why am I afraid of that pleasure, since it is a pleasure that has nothing to do with sensual desires and unwholesome states?’
mn100:29.4: ‘I am not afraid of that pleasure, since it is a pleasure that has nothing to do with sensual desires and unwholesome states.’
mn100:30.2: ‘It is not easy to attain that pleasure with a body so extremely emaciated.
mn100:30.3: Suppose I were to eat some solid food, some boiled rice and porridge?’
mn100:30.4: So I ate some solid food, some boiled rice and porridge.
mn100:30.5: Now at that time, Bhāradvāja, five bhikkhus were attending on me, thinking:
mn100:30.6: ‘Whatever truth the ascetic Gotama attains, he will tell us.’
mn100:30.7: But when I ate the solid food, the boiled rice and porridge, the group of five bhikkhus were disgusted and left me, saying:
mn100:30.8: ‘The ascetic Gotama has become self-indulgent; he has given up striving and reverted to luxury.’
mn100:31-33.1: Then, Bhāradvāja, having eaten solid food and regained strength, quite secluded from sensual desires … I entered upon and abided in the first jhāna.
mn100:31-33.2: With the stilling of initial and sustained application, I entered upon and abided in the second jhāna, which has internal placidity and singleness of mind, without initial application, without sustained application, with joy and pleasure born of concentration …
mn100:31-33.4: I entered upon and abided in the fourth jhāna.
mn100:34.1: When my mind was thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of imperfection, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, I directed it, inclined it, to the knowledge of recollection of past lives.
mn100:34.2: I recollected my manifold past lives, that is, one birth, two births … thus with their aspects and particulars I recollected my manifold past lives.
mn100:35.1: This, Bhāradvāja, was the first true knowledge attained by me in the first watch of the night;
mn100:35.2: ignorance was banished and true knowledge arose; darkness was banished and light arose, as happens in one who abides diligent, ardent, and self-controlled.
mn100:36-38.1: When my mind was thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of imperfection, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, I directed it, inclined it, to the knowledge of the passing away and reappearance of beings.
mn100:36-38.2: With the divine eye, purified and surpassing the human, I saw beings passing away and reappearing, inferior and superior, fair and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate; I understood how beings pass on according to their actions …
mn100:36-38.3: this, Bhāradvāja, was the second true knowledge attained by me in the middle watch of the night;
mn100:36-38.4: ignorance was banished and true knowledge arose; darkness was banished and light arose, as happens in one who abides diligent, ardent, and self-controlled.
mn100:39.1: When my mind was thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of imperfection, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, I directed it, inclined it, to the knowledge of the exhaustion of the taints.
mn100:39.2: I directly knew as it actually is: ‘This is suffering’; I directly knew as it actually is: ‘This is the origin of suffering’; I directly knew as it actually is: ‘This is the cessation of suffering’; I directly knew as it actually is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering’;
mn100:39.3: I directly knew as it actually is: ‘These are the taints’; I directly knew as it actually is: ‘This is the origin of the taints’; I directly knew as it actually is: ‘This is the cessation of the taints’; I directly knew as it actually is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of the taints.’
mn100:40.1: Knowing and seeing thus, my mind was liberated from the taint of sensual desire, liberated from the taint of being, liberated from the taint of ignorance.
mn100:40.2: When it was liberated, there came the knowledge: ‘It is liberated.’
mn100:40.3: I directly knew: ‘Birth is exhausted, the life divine has been lived, what was to be done is done, there is no more of this to come.’
mn100:41.1: This, Bhāradvāja, was the third true knowledge attained by me in the last watch of the night;
mn100:41.2: ignorance was banished and true knowledge arose; darkness was banished and light arose, as happens in one who abides diligent, ardent, and self-controlled.”
mn100:42.1: When this was said, the student Saṅgārava said to the Blessed One:
mn100:42.2: “Master Gotama’s striving was the striving of one who does not falter, Master Gotama’s striving was the striving of a true man,[^2]
mn100:42.3: as befits an Arahant, a Fully Enlightened One.
mn100:42.4: But, Master Gotama, are there gods?”[^3]
mn100:42.5: “It is known to me, Bhāradvāja, on good grounds, that—
mn100:42.7: “How is it, Master Gotama, that when asked ‘are there gods?’ you say: ‘It is known to me, Bhāradvāja, on good grounds, that there are gods’?
mn100:42.8: Is that not, Master Gotama, in that case empty and false?”
mn100:42.9: “Bhāradvāja, when asked ‘are there gods?’, whether one says ‘there are gods’, or whether one says ‘it is known to me on good grounds’,
mn100:42.10: in either case a wise man should come to the definite conclusion here:
mn100:42.12: “Then why did Master Gotama not answer me in that way from the start?”
mn100:42.13: “It is widely accepted in the world, Bhāradvāja, that—
mn100:43.1: When this was said, the student Saṅgārava said to the Blessed One:
mn100:43.3: As though he were righting the overthrown, revealing the hidden, showing the way to one who was lost, or holding up a lamp in the darkness so that those with eyes could see forms—so too the Dhamma has been made clear in many ways by Master Gotama.
mn100:43.4: I go to Master Gotama for refuge, and to the Dhamma, and to the Sangha of bhikkhus.
mn100:43.5: Let Master Gotama remember me as a lay follower who has gone to him for refuge from today for life.”
mn100:45.1: The householder chapter, the bhikkhu chapter,
mn100:45.3: the king chapter, and the brahmin chapter—
mn100:45.4: these five are in the Majjhima collection.
